series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested reverting commit 9a42aed48421, which prefers nonfull over free clusters for small order allocations, and instead always scanning full clusters to prioritize contiguity on large physical swap devices.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

That's a interesting problem. I think the real problem is with commit
9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters"), right?

It's more like a balance between fragmentation and contiguity of small
order allocation issue.

Perhaps we should instead always scan the full clusters and revert
that one commit? That commit was only following the idea of keeping
the allocation more compacted for that series, it looked good at that
time. Since fragmentation issues can be solved in other ways,
contiguity seems to matter more for large physical swap devices.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a reclaim batch spans multiple non-full clusters, which can lead to scattered writes and readahead requests.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti expressed interest in the proposed solution and asked for more information about alternative fragmentation solutions.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Kairui,

On Thu, Oct 22, 2026 at 5:27 PM Kairui Song <ryncsn@gmail.com> wrote:

---

Oh, okay. I thought reverting it wasn't an option given the good
numbers the patch provides.

What are the other fragmentation solutions you are referring to?

Thanks,

Alex

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the proposed solution of allocating contiguous swap slots may not address the underlying issue and could lead to increased memory overhead, scanning overhead, etc., suggesting that physical swap space compaction is still a problem and virtual swap space would just shift the issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hmm what other way are you thinking of? Physical swap space compaction
requires vswap, which has not landed. And we'd just be kicking the
problem to virtual swap space. Sure, we won't be failing allocation,
but that would still increase the memory overhead, scanning overhead,
etc.

I encountered this myself. Remember when I wrote my own swap allocator
for vswap? In one of the version, I went for free clusters first
instead of partial clusters. It fragmented the swap space, so I had to
copy your homework and went for partially used clusters first...

Anyway, maybe I'm wrong - some numbers would be nice here.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed support for the patch, noting that there are still workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested that the swap subsystem be made to work for them.

The reviewer agrees with the patch's approach of allocating contiguous swap slots, noting that it makes sense to not apply the heuristic for large folios.

Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the patch's approach of preferring non-full clusters over free clusters may lead to increased lock contention and fragmentation in swap files, but believes it will be fine as long as contiguity is found for the first time in the batch.

Reviewer Nhat Pham questioned the effectiveness of the patch's approach, noting that it may constantly overshoot the estimate of pages to be reclaimed due to rotating/promoting references, which could create problems down the line. He suggested collecting a batch of pages after unmapping and passing them to the phys swap allocator as an alternative solution.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] cgroup/cpuset: check effective mems for a movable-only configuration

version_history.subject: [PATCH] cgroup/cpuset: check effective mems for a movable-only configuration

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the cgroup/cpuset code to check for effective memory settings in a movable-only configuration. The change moves the check from the hotplug path to the update_nodemasks_hier function, where it can be performed more accurately. This prevents warnings when a task requests a movable node that is not present in its parent's nodemask, but will still warn if the parent's mems include the node later. The patch also removes an unnecessary check in the update_nodemask function.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH 2/2] sched: use static_branch_likely() for the NUMA balancing tick check
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch proposes to use static_branch_likely() for the NUMA balancing tick check, aligning it with other instances in the code.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (Meta)
review_comments.summary: Identified that this instance is inconsistent with other places in the code. Suggested alignment for consistency.

review_comments.author: Vincent Guittot
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the inconsistency and suggested using unlikely() instead of likely(). Mentioned that others are also shipped enabled by default.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, 23 Oct 2026 at 17:21, Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:
>
> On 2026-10-23 14:23 +0200, Vincent Guittot wrote:
> > On Fri, 23 Oct 2026 at 04:31, Yafang Shao <laoar.shao@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > task_tick_fair() checks sched_numa_balancing on every tick. The
> > > static_branch_unlikely() annotation reserves the nop for the disabled case,
> > > so the default configuration (NUMA_BALANCING_DEFAULT_ENABLED=y) pays a
> > > taken jump per tick. Flip the polarity to static_branch_likely() so that
> > > the fast path matches the default.
> > >
> > > Signed-off-by: Yafang Shao <laoar.shao@gmail.com>
> > > Acked-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
> > > ---
> > >  kernel/sched/fair.c | 2 +-
> > >  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
> > >
> > > diff --git a/kernel/sched/fair.c b/kernel/sched/fair.c
> > > index 973647ad6c2d..71dc47d6114d 100644
> > > --- a/kernel/sched/fair.c
> > > +++ b/kernel/sched/fair.c
> > > @@ -15351,7 +15351,7 @@ static void task_tick_fair(struct rq *rq, struct task_struct *curr, int queued)
> > >         if (queued)
> > >                 return;
> > >
> > > -       if (static_branch_unlikely(&sched_numa_balancing))
> > > +       if (static_branch_likely(&sched_numa_balancing))
> >
> > static_branch_unlikely is used by default for other static keys too
> > like  sched_cluster_active, sched_cache_active, __sched_core_enabled
> > sched_asym_cpucapacity and others ...
>
> every other instance checking sched_numa_balancing checks likely(), this
> is the odd one out.

Some other places might be behind another key but otherwise it should
be unlikely()

>
> > So systems which don't enable them don't pay a jump when not using it.
> > I don't see why numa should be different
> >
>
> numa balancing ships enabled by default.

Others are also shipped enabled by default

>
> This just looks like cleanup to me.
>
> --
> ~Gregory
>
